body:
When prior environmental clearance is required

Under the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006, specified projects and activities require prior environmental clearance before the activity covered by the notification is undertaken. The notification includes listed new projects and certain expansions, modernisations or changes in product mix that meet its conditions.

The purpose is to examine likely environmental effects before major decisions become difficult to reverse. Appraisal may consider air and water impacts, waste, land use, nearby settlements, ecological sensitivity and proposed safeguards.

Not every factory, construction activity or industrial plot automatically requires prior EC. The starting point is whether the proposal falls within the EIA Notification's applicable schedule, thresholds and conditions.

Category A and Category B

CategoryExpert appraisalEC decision
ACentral Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC)MoEFCC or the competent central authority
BAppropriate State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC)State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA)

Category assignment depends on the project's type, size, location and applicable conditions. A project that would otherwise be Category B can fall under central appraisal when a relevant general condition of the notification applies. Where this condition applies, Category B projects within 5 km of protected areas, CPCB-identified critically polluted areas, notified eco-sensitive areas or inter-State or international boundaries undergo Category A appraisal (10 km for river-valley, thermal-power, industrial-estate and common hazardous-waste treatment, storage and disposal projects), while the respective States or Union Territories may agree to reduce or waive the inter-State boundary distance.

In Gujarat, SEAC examines and recommends on projects within its notified jurisdiction, whereas SEIAA makes the environmental-clearance decision. These are separate roles. SEIAA does not become the pollution-control board merely because it considers pollution-related impacts.

The essential stages of environmental appraisal

  1. Screening: For applicable Category B proposals, determining whether the proposal is B1 or B2 and what level of assessment is required.
  2. Scoping: Identifying significant impacts to study and setting the terms of reference for an EIA study where required.
  3. Public consultation: Seeking views of affected persons and other stakeholders for projects to which this requirement applies.
  4. Appraisal: Examining the application, environmental information, consultation outcomes and proposed safeguards before recommending a decision.

These are the main stages described in the 2006 framework; all 4 stages do not apply to every project. Category B1 proposals generally require a detailed EIA study, while B2 proposals do not require that report under the basic classification. Public-consultation requirements also depend on the applicable provisions and exemptions.

GPCB's role during public consultation

For projects requiring a public hearing under the notification, the concerned State Pollution Control Board conducts the prescribed hearing arrangements. In Gujarat, this is a role of GPCB. The draft EIA report is made available for public responses, with at least 30 days' notice of the hearing. The hearing records environmental concerns and suggestions; it does not itself grant EC. The appraisal and final decision remain with the competent EIA authorities.

Gujarat's state appraisal institutions

The central government reconstituted SEIAA, Gujarat through S.O. 3895(E), dated 11 September 2024, for a 3-year term from publication. A Gujarat SEAC was reconstituted through S.O. 4355(E), dated 6 August 2026, for a 4-year term. That 2026 SEAC notification covers non-mining appraisal; mining proposals must follow their applicable designated arrangements. The basic distinction remains: expert appraisal supplies recommendations, while the competent authority decides on EC.

EC and pollution consent after the 2024 changes

Because of the November 2024 notifications, a project requiring and obtaining EC is exempt from obtaining a separate CTE under the Water and Air Acts. Pollution-control considerations are integrated into the EC procedure, with GPCB's input. CTO remains a separate operational requirement where applicable.

For example, environmental clearance for an industrial estate does not automatically prove that every future individual unit has satisfied its own operating consent, hazardous-waste or location-specific legal obligations. The precise conditions of the estate's approval and the proposed unit must be examined.

Prelims focus

  • EIA Notification: S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006.
  • Category A: central expert appraisal and central EC decision.
  • Category B: appropriate SEAC appraisal and SEIAA decision.
  • GPCB conducts prescribed public hearings; it does not decide EC.
  • Gujarat SEIAA was reconstituted in September 2024; a Gujarat SEAC was reconstituted in August 2026.
  • Trap: An expert appraisal committee recommends; the competent EC authority decides.

[Sources: MoEFCC, EIA Notification, S.O. 1533(E), 14 September 2006, paragraphs 2–7 and Schedule; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Parliamentary reply on environmental scrutiny, 8 December 2022; Gazette of India, S.O. 3895(E), 11 September 2024, reconstitution of SEIAA Gujarat; Gazette of India, S.O. 4355(E), 6 August 2026, reconstitution of Gujarat SEAC; MoEFCC, Lok Sabha reply, 3 February 2025. Sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Category A follows EAC to the central authority; Category B follows SEAC to SEIAA. GPCB conducts Gujarat public hearings but does not grant EC.
pictures.caption: Appraisal and clearance decisions follow different institutional paths.

title: Environmental Clearance in Gujarat: SEIAA, SEAC and GPCB

body:
Why Gujarat's coast needs separate regulation

Gujarat has extensive coastal areas, including the Gulfs of Kachchh and Khambhat. Coastal lands support ports, fishing settlements, salt-related activities, mangroves, wetlands and important marine habitats. Construction, dredging, land reclamation, industrial activity and pollution can affect these ecosystems and the livelihoods of coastal communities.

The Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) framework regulates specified development in coastal and marine areas. Its central purpose is to protect sensitive ecosystems, maintain coastal environmental quality and allow development only according to the conditions prescribed for the relevant location.

The legal framework

The CRZ Notification, 2019, G.S.R. 37(E), was issued on 18 January 2019 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It provides for coastal-area classification and regulates activities within notified CRZ boundaries. Until the revised CZMP under the 2019 notification is approved, appraisal and CRZ clearance continue under the 2011 notification and its approved CZMP.

The High Tide Line (HTL) is an important reference for CRZ demarcation. Along the sea front, the notification generally covers land up to 500 metres landward of the HTL, besides specified intertidal and marine areas. Different rules govern tidal-influenced water bodies such as connected creeks and estuaries. The applicable approved Coastal Zone Management Plan (CZMP) and the notification must be examined together; a simple 500-metre rule cannot decide every coastal case.

The main CRZ categories

ZoneBasic characterKey idea
CRZ-IEcologically sensitive and specified intertidal areasStrong protection; only specifically permitted regulated activities
CRZ-IIDeveloped coastal areas meeting the notified criteriaDevelopment subject to applicable conditions
CRZ-IIIRelatively undeveloped coastal areasRegulated development and applicable no-development restrictions
CRZ-IVSpecified coastal and tidal water areasProtection and regulation of activities in water areas

CRZ-I includes sensitive features such as mangroves, coral reefs and sand dunes under the notification's detailed classification. A proposal cannot assume that activity permitted in a developed coastal area will also be permitted in an ecologically sensitive area.

What GCZMA does

The Gujarat Coastal Zone Management Authority (GCZMA) is the state authority responsible for important CRZ scrutiny, regulation and enforcement. It examines proposals against the applicable approved coastal-management plan and legal conditions. It may recommend proposals to the designated competent authority, monitor compliance and address violations using powers available under the Environment (Protection) Act.

The central government reconstituted GCZMA through S.O. 713(E), dated 11 February 2026, published on 12 February 2026. The order provides for a 3-year term, a 15-member authority and headquarters at Gandhinagar. Its membership brings together relevant state departments and bodies, including pollution-control, forest, maritime and fisheries institutions.

Under the 2026 order, GCZMA examines project applications in accordance with the applicable approved coastal-management plans and makes recommendations to the competent authority within the prescribed 60-day period from receipt of the proposals. This recommendation should not be confused with an independent, universal power to grant every type of project clearance.

District-level participation and enforcement

The CRZ Notification, 2019, makes State Governments or Union Territory coastal-zone authorities primarily responsible for enforcement and monitoring. It also provides for district-level committees chaired by the District Magistrate, including at least 3 representatives of traditional coastal communities, including fisherfolk. This arrangement recognises that coastal regulation affects people who depend directly on coastal resources.

Coastal approval does not replace other permissions

A proposed port-related facility may require CRZ scrutiny because of its location. Its industrial operations may separately require GPCB consent. If the activity is listed under the EIA Notification, prior EC may be required. Where a marine protected area or forest land is affected, wildlife or forest requirements may also apply.

Prelims focus

  • CRZ Notification, 2019: G.S.R. 37(E), dated 18 January 2019.
  • HTL is a central reference for coastal-zone demarcation.
  • CRZ-I is associated with ecologically sensitive coastal features.
  • GCZMA was reconstituted by S.O. 713(E), dated 11 February 2026, for 3 years.
  • District CRZ committees are chaired by the District Magistrate and include at least 3 traditional coastal-community representatives.
  • Trap: GCZMA scrutiny is not the same as GPCB pollution consent.

[Sources: MoEFCC, CRZ Notification, G.S.R. 37(E), 18 January 2019, paragraphs 1–5 and 9; Gazette of India, S.O. 713(E), 11 February 2026, published 12 February 2026, clauses on GCZMA composition, powers and functions; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, PIB explanation of CRZ enforcement and district committees, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Fisherfolk tend nets beside wooden boats on Gujarat's coast, with mangroves lining a tidal creek and a commercial port in the distance.
pictures.caption: Coastal regulation protects habitats while considering coastal livelihoods.

pictures.alt: A coastal project's CZMP and CRZ zone guide GCZMA scrutiny and its 60-day recommendation, followed by permission, monitoring and separate applicable checks.
pictures.caption: Coastal location determines a separate regulatory check.

title: Gujarat Coastal Zone Management Authority and Coastal Clearances

body:
Why forest and wildlife approval is separate

Pollution control concerns emissions, effluents and environmental quality. Forest and wildlife laws additionally protect forests, habitats, species and designated protected areas. A project can meet pollution standards and still be legally restricted because of its location or ecological impact.

In Gujarat, this distinction matters around protected landscapes such as Gir and the Marine National Park in the Gulf of Kachchh. The applicable legal requirements depend on the precise site, protected-area status and proposed activity.

The state forest administration

The Forests and Environment Department, Government of Gujarat, handles state responsibilities relating to forests, wildlife and environmental administration. Forest management is carried out through the state's forest-administration structure, including the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests and field officers such as Divisional Forest Officers.

These officers are important when examining a project's likely effect on forest land, verifying its location and carrying out responsibilities under the forest laws. Their administrative roles do not mean that every field officer can independently approve the diversion of forest land.

Forest-land diversion and central approval

The law historically known as the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is now titled the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, following the 2023 amendments. Subject to the Act's scope and specific statutory exceptions, Section 2 requires prior approval of the Central Government before specified orders are made permitting forest land to be used for non-forest purposes.

The Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Rules, 2023, as amended, provide a procedure involving the project proponent, state authorities and central government. Forest-diversion approval ordinarily has 2 stages:

  1. Stage-I, or in-principle approval: Preliminary central approval subject to specified conditions.
  2. Stage-II, or final approval: Central approval following satisfactory compliance with the Stage-I conditions and the applicable procedure.

Conditions may include compensatory afforestation, prescribed payments and other forest-protection measures. Stage-I approval should not be mistaken for unconditional final permission. Any limited working permission must satisfy its separate legal conditions.

A local land-use approval, GPCB consent or EIA environmental clearance does not by itself replace the Central Government's forest approval where Section 2 applies.

Wildlife protection institutions

The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 provides important legal protection for wild animals, specified plants and protected areas such as national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. The state forest and wildlife administration implements many of its provisions.

Chief Wildlife Warden

The Chief Wildlife Warden is a principal statutory wildlife authority in the state. The office performs duties under the Wildlife Act, including responsibilities connected with protection, management and permissions that the Act assigns to it.

Gujarat State Board for Wildlife

Under Section 6 of the Wildlife Act, a State Board for Wildlife is constituted. The state's Chief Minister chairs the Board. The Gujarat government's reconstitution resolution of 13 July 2023 identifies the Chief Wildlife Warden as Member Secretary.

Under Section 8, a State Board for Wildlife advises the state government on selecting and managing protected areas, wildlife-conservation policy and other specified matters. It is not simply another name for the Forest Department or GPCB.

The National Board for Wildlife is a distinct national institution chaired by the Prime Minister. Certain proposals affecting protected areas require additional wildlife consideration under the applicable legal framework. The exact recommendation and approval route depends on the proposed activity and location.

Forest land and wildlife areas are different legal questions

Forest diversion asks whether covered forest land may be used for a non-forest purpose. Wildlife scrutiny asks whether an activity affecting a protected area or its regulated surroundings is permissible under wildlife and related laws. A project may require one, both or neither, depending on its location and nature.

Prelims focus

  • Wild Life (Protection) Act: 1972.
  • Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, is now titled Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.
  • Section 2 of the forest law requires prior Central Government approval for covered forest-land diversion.
  • Forest approval ordinarily involves Stage-I and Stage-II.
  • The Chief Minister chairs the State Board for Wildlife; Section 8 concerns its advisory duties.
  • Trap: State Forest Department scrutiny is not the same as final central forest-diversion approval.

[Sources: Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, Sections 1A and 2; Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Rules, 2023, Rule 9, and Amendment Rules, 2025; Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, Sections 6 and 8; Government of Gujarat, Forests and Environment Department, Resolution VPS/102017/1872/W, 13 July 2023, Constitution of Gujarat State Board for Wildlife; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 7, Conservation of Plants and Animals. Official sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Forest proposals follow a state-to-central approval route; wildlife wardens and State and National Boards have distinct statutory and advisory roles.
pictures.caption: Forest-diversion and wildlife-protection responsibilities are distinct.
